analytic.title: An Efficient Zero-Laxity Based Real-Time Multiprocessor Scheduling Algorithm

div.p: In this paper, we present an efficient global real-time multiprocessor scheduling algorithm based on the beneficial Zero-Laxity policy. The algorithm selects tasks for execution based on their execution requirements.

Tasks with largest execution requirements are always scheduled first; however when a task reaches zero laxity it is given the highest priority and executed until completion. The simulation showed that the proposed algorithm misses few deadlines and achieves high schedulability levels compared to currently existing zero laxity based algorithms.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems the correctness of an operation does not depend on its logical correctness only; but also the time at which the results are produced. Realtime systems are classified into three different classes based on their timing constraints [1].

div.head: Hard Real-time Systems
div.p: In hard real-time systems, missing a deadline results in a system failure and may even leads to a catastrophic failure.

div.head: Firm Real-time Systems
div.p: Firm real-time systems have hard constraints; but it can tolerate infrequent deadline misses at the expense of degradation of quality of service.

div.head: Soft Real-time Systems
div.p: Soft real-time systems can tolerate with deadline misses; however the missed deadlines degraded the system performance in terms of quality of service.

Scheduling of real-time tasks on multiprocessor system can be broadly classified into two main categories: partitioned and global. In partitioned scheduling, tasks are allocated to processors statically, and each processor schedules its allocated tasks independently using uniprocessor scheduling algorithms. The advantage of partitioned scheduling is that it reduces the multiprocessor scheduling problem to a uniprocessor ones which are extensively studied and well-known to be optimal. However, there are two disadvantages of this category. The first one is that, finding an optimal allocation of tasks to processors is known to be a bin-packing problem, which is NP-hard, and due to this tasks are usually assigned to processors using non-optimal heuristics. The second one is that there exists task systems that can only be schedulable if and only if tasks are not partitioned. Despite this, partitioning approaches are still widely used by system designers [2,3].

In global scheduling, tasks are prioritized in a global priority queue and are allowed to migrate between processors. The scheduler then selects the highest priority tasks for execution. Unluckily, scheduling algorithms that are known to be optimal for uniprocessor systems, such as the Least Laxity First, Rate-Monotonic (RM) and Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) algorithms cannot be used here because they produce low processors utilization. However, recently there has been an interest in global scheduling due to the inefficiencies of partitioned scheduling algorithms. [4][5][6][7][8].

One of the efficient real-time multiprocessor scheduling algorithm is Earliest Deadline until Zero Laxity (EDZL) which is a global hybrid scheduler that provides an improvement of its predecessor Earliest Deadline First (EDF) by exploiting the beneficial Zero Laxity policy. In this paper, we propose Largest Execution until Zero Laxity (LEZL) which prioritized tasks according to largest execution first; however when a task reaches zero laxity it is given highest priority and is executed until completion.
We show that our new proposed algorithm (LEZL) outperforms EDZL in terms of deadline misses as well as schedulability.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: In Section II we describe the task model and define the terms that will be used in this paper. Section III reviews related work. Section IV explains the new algorithm with an example to show how the algorithm works. Section V shows and discusses the simulated results. Lastly we conclude in section VII and show further future work.

div.head: II. MODEL AND TERMS DEFINITION
div.p: This paper considers the scheduling of n periodic tasks with implicit deadlines on a platform of m Symmetric Shared-Memory multiprocessor (SMP). A periodic task, in real-time systems, is a task that is periodically released at a constant rate. Usually, two parameters are used to describe a periodic task T i ; its execution requirement e i as well as its period p i . An instance of a periodic task (i.e. release) is known as a job and is described as T i, j = (e i , p i ) where j=1, 2, 3, … . The deadline of a job is the arrival time of its successor. div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: Real-time systems require the use of optimized algorithms as well as strategies in order to obey their timing constraints. To meet the timing constraints of real-time systems, such algorithms and strategies give higher priority to tasks using a decision that appears to be the best at the moment, and hence they are called greedy algorithms. The well-known used greedy criteria's are the earliest deadline first, the least laxity first, and the shorter period first. Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm [9] is an example of the first strategy, which gives priority to tasks with earliest deadline. An example of an algorithm that uses the second greedy criteria is the Least Laxity First (LLF) [10]. The algorithm that uses the third criteria is Rate-Monotonic (RM) [11].

The difference in the above mentioned three algorithms is in the complexity of their priority policy as well as their capability to meet the timing restrictions [2]. Although these algorithms known to be optimal for scheduling of real-time tasks on uniprocessor systems, but their performance in terms of schedulability degraded when they are extended to schedule real-time tasks in multiprocessors systems. Figures Fig. 1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 below shows the schedules generated by the three mentioned algorithms for the feasible taskset {t 1 (3, 5) and t 2 (4, 10)} in a system with one processor. The authors in [12] have shown that the laxity of a task is an important parameter that considers both urgency and parallelism together when making a scheduling decision. A good example of such laxity based algorithms is EDZL (Earliest Deadline first until Zero Laxity) [13] which extends EDF by giving tasks with zero laxity highest priority and executes them until completion without interruption. It has been shown that EDZL dominates EDF [14].

div.head: IV. PROPOSED ALGORITHM
div.p: As being mentioned previously; our proposed algorithm LEZL prioritize tasks based on their execution requirements. Tasks with largest execution requirements have higher priority and always are scheduled for execution first; however once a task reaches zero laxity it is given highest priority and is scheduled for execution immediately and run until completion without any interruption. Furthermore, when a task reaches zero laxity, our proposed LEZL algorithm preempts the task with the maximum laxity for it; unlike EDZL which preempts the task with largest deadline. Preempting the task with the maximum laxity, i.e. one that has largest idle time to wait before reaching zero laxity, give the scheduler more time to run other tasks before the preempted task reaches zero laxity; however preempting the task with the largest deadline doesn't necessary mean that it has a large idle time since it can have the largest deadline and at the same time has a large execution requirement; and thus once preempted sooner it became critical. div.head: V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
div.p: To test our proposed algorithm, we have conducted an extensive experimental work. We have generated random tasksets for 2, 4, and 8 processors with variable size n where n>m. For each processor, we have generated 100,000 tasksets using a uniform distribution. The results that we obtained were encouraging in terms of deadline misses as well as schedulability. Fig. 5 below shows the average deadline misses per task for the proposed LEZL algorithm compared to EDZL and G-EDF. In Fig. 6 below, we also show the percentage of the scheduled tasksets for the proposed algorithm against both EDZL and G-EDF. It can be clearly seen from both Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 that our proposed LEZL algorithm outperforms both EDZL and G-EDF. To verify the significant improvement in terms of deadline misses as well as schedulability of our proposed LEZL algorithm against EDZL, we have conducted an independent sample t-test. The t-test reported a significant reduction in deadline misses as well a significant increase in schedulability of LEZL against EDZL with α=0.05.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presented an efficient soft real-time multiprocessor scheduling algorithm. The proposed algorithm gives higher priority to tasks with large execution requirement. However, tasks with zero laxity are given the highest priority and allowed to execute until completion without any interruption. The simulation showed that the proposed algorithm misses few deadlines as well as achieves high schedulability compared to EDZL, the state-of-the-art zero laxity based algorithm. The significance of the obtained results were successfully verified using the Student t-test.
